sentences.say: Alder is just behind, at minus zero point six five, from thirty patients.

sentences.text: If you had to bet on which clinic is truly the worst, would you still pick Dune?

segments.visual: Faint arrows from every estimate toward the centre line, longest for the clinics with fewest patients.

sentences.text: Many analysts would not. They would pull every estimate toward the average, and pull hardest where there is least to go on.
That is the random-effect model, and this episode is about what it buys and what it costs.

segments.visual: Series logo and wordmark; arc and episode title.

sentences.text: Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: fixed or random?

segments.visual: Left: four separate dots, labelled fixed: nothing assumed. Right: the same dots under one bell curve with a centre and a spread, labelled random: draws from one curve.

sentences.text: So far, each provider has had a number of its own, and we have assumed nothing about those numbers. That is what fixed means.
The alternative assumes something: that the numbers are draws from one bell curve, with a centre and a spread.

segments.visual: Dune's estimate joined to the centre by a band. The formula for reliability: spread squared over spread squared plus standard error squared. With 0.33 and 0.66: 0.20.

sentences.text: Then each estimate is a compromise between the provider's own data and the centre. The weight on its own data is called its reliability.
For Dune, with a spread of 0.33 borrowed from our crowd, the reliability is 0.20. Dune keeps a fifth of its distance from the centre.
sentences.say: For Dune, with a spread of zero point three three borrowed from our crowd, the reliability is zero point two. Dune keeps a fifth of its distance from the centre.

segments.visual: All five clinics, before and after the pull: Dune −0.58 to −1.33, Alder −0.65 to −1.18, Birch −1.82 to −1.65, Cedar unmoved at −1.52, and Elm, which had none, at −1.71.

sentences.text: Do that for every clinic. Dune moves to minus 1.33. Alder, with more patients, keeps two fifths, and stops at minus 1.18.
sentences.say: Do that for every clinic. Dune moves to minus one point three three. Alder, with more patients, keeps two fifths, and stops at minus one point one eight.

sentences.text: The order has flipped. And Elm, which had no estimate at all, now has one.

segments.visual: The two hundred providers by number of patients. For each, a line from its fixed-effect estimate to its random-effect one. The lines are long on the left and short on the right.

sentences.text: Now the crowd of two hundred, fitted both ways. Each line joins a provider's fixed-effect estimate to its random-effect one.
Small providers move most. Under 50 patients, a typical reliability is 0.37. Above 200, it is 0.83.
sentences.say: Small providers move most. Under fifty patients, a typical reliability is zero point three seven. Above two hundred, it is zero point eight three.

segments.visual: Three piles of two hundred values: fixed-effect estimates, spread 0.44; the truth, 0.33; random-effect estimates, 0.26.

sentences.text: The estimates draw together. Their spread falls from 0.44 to 0.26.
sentences.say: The estimates draw together. Their spread falls from zero point four four to zero point two six.

sentences.text: The true spread is 0.33. Fixed effects scatter wider than the truth; random effects, narrower.
sentences.say: The true spread is zero point three three. Fixed effects scatter wider than the truth; random effects, narrower.

segments.visual: Each provider's error against its number of patients, for both fits. Bars for the typical error: 0.28 and 0.20 overall; 0.40 and 0.25 under 50 patients.

sentences.text: What does the pull buy? Accuracy, on average. We know the truth in this crowd, so we can measure the typical error.
It falls from 0.28 to 0.20. For providers under 50 patients, from 0.40 to 0.25.
sentences.say: It falls from zero point two eight to zero point two. For providers under fifty patients, from zero point four to zero point two five.

segments.visual: The six planted providers on a line marked at 0.8 either side of the centre. Their fixed-effect estimates average 0.67 from the centre; their random-effect ones, 0.46. Flags: four and three.

sentences.text: Now the costs. First, the pull does not know who truly differs. Our six planted providers sit 0.8 from the centre.
sentences.say: Now the costs. First, the pull does not know who truly differs. Our six planted providers sit zero point eight from the centre.

sentences.text: Fixed effects put them at 0.67, on average. Random effects, at 0.46.
sentences.say: Fixed effects put them at zero point six seven, on average. Random effects, at zero point four six.

sentences.text: And fixed effects flag four of the six; random effects, three.

scenes.chapter: What it costs: the case mix

segments.visual: True provider effects against case mix: a downward cloud. Providers with sicker patients truly do better.

sentences.text: The second cost is subtler. In this crowd, providers with sicker patients truly perform better. The random-effect model assumes there is no such link, and pulls everyone toward one centre.

segments.visual: Each provider's error against its case mix, two panels. Fixed effects: a level cloud, correlation 0.06. Random effects: a rising cloud, 0.35; the sickest fifth 0.10 too high, the healthiest 0.10 too low.

sentences.text: So its errors follow the case mix. Their correlation with it is 0.35. For fixed effects, 0.06.
sentences.say: So its errors follow the case mix. Their correlation with it is zero point three five. For fixed effects, zero point zero six.

sentences.text: The sickest fifth of providers look 0.10 worse than they are. The healthiest fifth, 0.10 better.
sentences.say: The sickest fifth of providers look zero point one worse than they are. The healthiest fifth, zero point one better.

segments.visual: The random-effect panel again, for the same crowd with the link broken: a level cloud, correlation −0.01.

sentences.text: Break the link, so that performance and case mix are unrelated, and that correlation vanishes.

segments.visual: Two cards. Fixed effects: judging individual providers, when performance may be tied to case mix. Random effects: many tiny providers, or questions about providers as a population.

sentences.text: So which? If you are judging individual providers, and performance may be tied to case mix, fixed effects.
If you have many tiny providers, or your question is about providers as a population, random effects.

segments.visual: Both cards feed one box: the standardization of Episode 11, observed over expected. Under it, a caution that applies to both: a risk factor nobody recorded.

sentences.text: Either way, the estimates feed the same standardization from Episode 11. The choice changes the numbers that go in, not the arithmetic that follows.
sentences.say: Either way, the estimates feed the same standardization from Episode eleven. The choice changes the numbers that go in, not the arithmetic that follows.

sentences.text: And neither one protects you from a risk factor that nobody recorded.

segments.visual: Three recap cards, each with a small icon.

sentences.text: Let's gather it up.
Random effects pull each estimate toward the centre, by its reliability.
The pull buys accuracy on average, and gives every provider an estimate.
It costs you the outliers, and it bends with the case mix.

segments.visual: A long row of small intercept markers, one per provider, running off the edge of the frame. The next episode's title.

sentences.text: Fixed effects have a cost of their own that we have not faced. One intercept per provider is a great many intercepts.
Next time: too many intercepts.
